10970:
"Murky" describes something that is dark, dirty, and unclear in a way that makes it hard to see through — or to understand. Picture a pond where someone just stirred up all the mud at the bottom. The water instantly becomes dark, thick, and cloudy. You can't see anything beneath the surface. That is the perfect image of murky.

But murky isn't just about water. It works across three distinct situations, and understanding all three will give you complete mastery of the word.
Meaning 1: Physical — Dark, Cloudy, and Hard to See Through

When murky describes something in the physical world, it means the thing is dark, dense, and obscured — usually because of dirt, pollution, sediment, smoke, or fog that is clouding it.

The murky river made it impossible to see the bottom. We swam cautiously through the murky lake. The city was blanketed in a murky haze of smoke and fog. He stared into the murky depths of the cave, unable to see what lay beyond.

Notice how murky always carries a slightly uncomfortable feeling. It's not just "a little dark" or "a little cloudy." There is something unsettling about it — you can't see what's there, and that unknowing creates unease.

This brings up an important distinction. "Dark" simply means there is little light — a dark room can still be clean and perfectly clear. "Cloudy" simply means not transparent — a glass of cloudy lemonade is just a bit thick. But murky combines darkness, cloudiness, and a sense of dirtiness or thickness, all wrapped in a feeling that something unpleasant might be lurking beneath the surface. That's what makes it a richer and more powerful word.
Meaning 2: Intellectual — Confusing, Vague, and Hard to Understand

Here, murky moves away from the physical world and into the world of ideas, situations, and explanations. When something is murky in this sense, it means it is unclear, confusing, and hard to make sense of — exactly as murky water makes it hard to see.

The company's financial situation is murky — nobody can tell what is really going on. The rules of this agreement are murky; I have read them three times and I still don't understand them. The line between what is legal and what is not is murky in this area of law. His explanation was so murky that everyone left the meeting more confused than before.

This is an extremely common usage. Whenever a situation has no clear answer, whenever an explanation raises more questions than it settles, whenever you sense there is more going on than what you can see — you can confidently call it murky.
Meaning 3: Moral — Suspicious, Shady, and Questionable

The third meaning of murky is about morality, reputation, and integrity. When someone's past, dealings, or actions are described as murky, it means they are suspicious, ethically questionable, or not entirely honest — perhaps involving wrongdoing, perhaps just things the person or organisation would prefer to keep hidden.

The politician had a murky past that he tried desperately to conceal. The business deal involved some murky financial transactions that nobody could quite explain. The company's murky ties to organised crime eventually came to light.

In this sense, murky implies that something is not clean. Just as murky water has dirt floating in it, a murky history has some kind of "dirt" — secrets, dishonesty, or wrongdoing. Importantly, you do not call something murky just because it is private. Murky carries the suggestion of something being wrong or suspicious, not merely undisclosed.
The Emotional Tone of the Word

Across all three of its meanings, murky is never a neutral word. It always creates a feeling of unease, mystery, and quiet discomfort. Think of the sensation of stepping into deep water without knowing what lies beneath, or listening to an explanation that does not quite add up, or sensing that something is wrong but not being able to prove it.

This emotional weight is precisely why murky appears so often in literature, journalism, and storytelling. It does not just describe — it evokes. It pulls readers into the uncertainty and the darkness of whatever is being described.

Murky sits in the moderate-to-strong range of intensity. It is noticeably stronger than mild words like "hazy" or "slightly unclear," but it is not the most extreme option available. Here is a rough sense of the scale for physical obscurity:

Slightly unclear → Hazy → Murky → Opaque (completely impossible to see through)

That middle position is useful — murky is serious and atmospheric without being over-the-top.
Words You Will Often See Alongside "Murky"

Murky almost always appears directly before a noun. The most common pairings across all three meanings are:

In the physical sense: murky water, murky depths, murky river, murky skies.

In the intellectual sense: murky situation, murky territory, murky logic, murky thinking. One phrase worth knowing especially well is "murky waters" — this is widely used as a figure of speech meaning a situation that is uncertain, risky, or confusing. "We are treading in murky waters with this new policy."

In the moral sense: murky past, murky history, murky dealings, murky ties, murky background.

No matter which meaning you encounter, murky always signals a lack of clarity that creates discomfort — whether you cannot see through something physically, cannot understand something intellectually, or cannot trust something morally. Whatever it is attached to, murky sends the same underlying message: something here is dark, unclear, and a little troubling.
10971:
A murmur is a soft, low, gentle, and continuous sound — one that is quiet enough that you have to pay attention to hear it, and often indistinct enough that you cannot make out every detail clearly. Think of it as sound that flows rather than hits you.

Three qualities define almost every use of this word:

  • Soft — never loud or harsh
  • Low-pitched — not sharp or shrill
  • Continuous or flowing — not a sudden bang or click, but something that lingers or runs

1. A gentle, flowing sound in nature or the environment

This is the most basic use. When something produces a quiet, soothing, running sound, that sound is a murmur.

  • The murmur of a stream — water flowing quietly over rocks
  • The murmur of the wind through the trees
  • The murmur of the ocean in the distance

These sounds share something: they are all soft, they keep going (they don't stop and start sharply), and they blend into the background rather than demanding your attention. You hear a murmur; you don't get startled by one.

2. A quiet, indistinct sound of many voices

When a group of people are all talking at the same time but no one is speaking loudly, the combined sound they make is a murmur. You know voices are there, but you cannot clearly make out what anyone is saying.

  • "A murmur ran through the audience when the speaker paused."
  • "From the other room, she could hear the murmur of a conversation."

Notice the feeling here: it is not silence, but it is not clear speech either. A murmur of voices sits somewhere in between — present, yet blurry.

3. A very soft way of speaking

When a single person speaks extremely softly — gently, almost under their breath — what they say can also be called a murmur. Here, "a murmur" refers to a quiet utterance, not just background noise.

  • "'I love you,' she said in a murmur."
  • "His reply was barely a murmur — she had to lean in to hear him."

This is subtly different from a whisper. A whisper is deliberately hushed — you choose to whisper to keep something secret, or to avoid disturbing others. A murmur, on the other hand, often suggests something more effortless and natural: a voice that is soft out of tenderness, tiredness, shyness, or simply because the moment calls for quiet. A murmur feels more intimate and unguarded than a whisper.

4. A quiet, restrained expression of dissatisfaction or complaint

When people are unhappy about something but do not openly protest — instead grumbling quietly among themselves — those quiet expressions of discontent are called murmurs.

  • "There were murmurs of disapproval from the crowd."
  • "The new policy was met with murmurs of protest."

This meaning captures something important about human behaviour: sometimes people are unhappy but are not willing (or not brave enough) to speak up loudly. A murmur of discontent is below the surface — it is real, but it has not yet broken into open argument or outcry. It suggests tension simmering quietly, not boiling over.

5. A heart murmur (medical use)

In medicine, a heart murmur is a specific term. When a doctor listens to your heart with a stethoscope, a healthy heart makes a rhythmic "lub-dub" sound. If there is an extra, unusual whooshing or swishing sound between those beats, that extra sound is called a murmur.

It is called a murmur because that is exactly what it sounds like to the doctor's ear — a soft, flowing, out-of-place noise. Heart murmurs are caused by turbulent blood flow inside the heart, and while some are harmless (called "innocent murmurs"), others can signal an underlying problem that needs attention.
The Thread That Connects All These Meanings

Whether you are talking about a stream, a crowd, a person's voice, a quiet complaint, or a sound inside the heart — a murmur is always:

  • Quiet (never forceful or loud)
  • Somewhat indistinct (you perceive it, but it is not sharp or perfectly clear)
  • Continuous or flowing (it runs or lingers rather than striking sharply)

These qualities give the word its character. A murmur feels gentle, soft-edged, and somewhat intimate or private. It is sound at low volume, hovering just at the edge of what you can clearly grasp.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Nearby wordHow it differs from "murmur"
WhisperIntentionally quiet to avoid being heard; more deliberate and secretive
HumA single steady musical tone; more monotone and tuneful
RumbleAlso low, but much louder and rougher — a rumble fills space, a murmur does not
RustleA dry, crackling sound (leaves, paper); has edges and texture, not the smooth flow of a murmur
GrumbleA complaint, but grumbles are louder and more openly irritated than murmurs

• The murmur of the brook outside the window helped her fall asleep.
  • He heard a murmur of voices behind the closed door but could not make out the words.
  • She thanked him in a murmur, too moved to speak clearly.
  • Murmurs of discontent spread through the factory workers after the announcement.
  • The doctor said the child had a small heart murmur but that it was nothing to worry about.

A murmur is a soft, low, continuous, and often indistinct sound — whether from nature, a group of voices, a person speaking gently, a quiet complaint, or an abnormal sound in the heart — and it always carries a sense of something gentle and present, but just below the threshold of full clarity or force.
10972: There are two meanings of this word, and both are worth knowing. One is spectacular. The other is quieter and more literary.
The main modern meaning: a flock of starlings in flight

A murmuration is the word for a flock of starlings — a common type of bird — when they gather in enormous numbers and move together through the sky in sweeping, swirling patterns. This isn't a handful of birds. A murmuration can involve tens of thousands, sometimes even a million starlings, all flying as one continuous, living shape.

Picture a vast dark cloud in the sky — but it's alive. It stretches outward, then suddenly pulls tight into a dense knot. It splits into two shapes, then merges back into one. It spirals like a whirlpool, then ripples outward like a wave. It moves with a kind of fluid grace that seems impossible for something made of individual creatures. From a distance, it looks less like a flock of birds and more like a single organism — like smoke being sculpted by invisible hands, or like a ribbon of silk billowing in slow motion.

The astonishing part is that no single bird is the leader. No bird is directing the others. Each starling simply watches the six or seven birds nearest to it and reacts to their movements almost instantly — matching their speed and direction within a fraction of a second. When one bird at the edge of the flock turns, that turn ripples through the entire mass faster than the human eye can process as separate moments. Scientists call this kind of result "emergent behaviour" — something complex and beautiful arising from each individual following very simple rules. The whole becomes something far greater than the sum of its parts.

Why do starlings do this? The primary reason is survival. A predator like a peregrine falcon can easily target one lone bird — it simply fixes its gaze on it and dives. But when a million birds are swirling in unpredictable, constantly shifting formations, the predator cannot lock onto any single target. The murmuration overwhelms and confuses it. The behaviour is also thought to help the birds share information about where to sleep for the night. Starlings roost together in large groups, and the evening murmuration seems to serve as a gathering ritual before they all descend to the same location together.

Murmurations typically happen in autumn and winter, in the hour before dusk. If you ever witness one in person, you'll notice something beyond what you see: a deep, rushing, whooshing sound — the combined beat of thousands of wings cutting through air at once. It is a sound unlike anything else.
The secondary, more literary meaning: the act or sound of murmuring

In its older and broader use, a murmuration simply refers to the sound or act of murmuring — a low, continuous, soft sound made by many voices or things together. You are most likely to encounter this meaning in literature rather than everyday conversation. A writer might describe "a murmuration of distant voices drifting through the open window," meaning a soft, blended hum of people murmuring in another room. Or "the murmuration of a brook over smooth stones," meaning the gentle, constant sound water makes as it runs. In this sense, the word sits alongside words like hum, drone, or whisper — it suggests something continuous, low, and unobtrusive.

This second meaning is rarely used in casual modern speech, but you will meet it in novels, poetry, and formal writing, so it is worth having in your vocabulary.

The connection between these two meanings is not a coincidence. When a murmuration of starlings passes close overhead, the sound it produces — thousands of wings all moving at once — is itself a kind of murmur: a deep, collective, rushing hum. The word carries both the visual spectacle and the sound it makes wrapped up together.

You would say: "We watched a murmuration of starlings transform the sky at sunset." Or: "A murmuration of hushed voices filled the waiting room." Or: "The murmuration lasted nearly twenty minutes before the birds finally settled into the trees." The word is always a noun and works exactly as you would expect any noun to work.

"Murmuration" is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful-sounding words in the English language. Its soft, rolling sounds mirror what it describes — something flowing, continuous, and gently overwhelming. It is the kind of word that feels like the thing it names. When you say it slowly, it almost sounds like a murmur itself.
10973:
A murrain is a deadly, fast-spreading disease — essentially a plague — that strikes animals, especially farm animals like cattle, sheep, horses, and pigs. Think of it as an epidemic, but one that tears through herds and flocks rather than through human populations.

The word almost always refers to a widespread outbreak, not just one sick animal. When a murrain struck a village in the Middle Ages, it could wipe out entire herds in a matter of weeks, devastating a farming community's livelihood in one blow.
What makes it different from just "animal disease"

The key idea packed into "murrain" is scale and devastation. It doesn't describe a single cow getting sick. It describes a catastrophic, contagious outbreak — the kind that spreads from farm to farm, kills most of the animals it touches, and leaves farmers with nothing.

In practice, the word has historically been used to describe real diseases we now have names for, such as:

  • Rinderpest — a catastrophic cattle plague that killed millions of animals across history
  • Anthrax — a lethal bacterial infection in livestock
  • Foot-and-mouth disease — a highly contagious viral disease in hoofed animals
  • Plague in sheep — various forms of pestilence

But people in earlier centuries didn't always know what disease was killing their animals. When the animals started dying in droves and no one could stop it, they simply called it a murrain. It was a catch-all word for "a devastating plague of animals."

The most famous appearance of this word is in the Bible, in the Book of Exodus. The fifth plague of Egypt — one of the ten plagues sent by God — is described as a murrain upon the Egyptians' livestock. It killed their cattle, horses, donkeys, camels, and sheep. This usage cemented the word's association with divine punishment, widespread death, and agricultural ruin.

This biblical connection is important because it's one reason the word carried such heavy weight for centuries. A murrain wasn't just bad luck — to people of that era, it felt like a curse from God.
The secondary use: as a curse

Because "murrain" meant a terrible plague, people in older times — particularly in the 1500s to 1700s — also used it as a mild curse or insult, similar to saying "a plague on you!" They might say:

"A murrain on you!"
"A murrain take him!"

This is the same pattern as other old curses — like "a pox on you" (referencing smallpox). You're essentially wishing a devastating disease upon someone, used as a colourful expression of anger or frustration. You'll encounter this use in Shakespeare's plays and other literature from that period.

Almost nobody in everyday conversation. Murrain is an archaic word — meaning it belongs to an older era of English and has largely fallen out of common use. You will encounter it mainly in:

  • The Bible (particularly older translations like the King James Version)
  • Shakespeare and other Renaissance/Elizabethan literature
  • Medieval and early modern historical texts
  • Historical novels set in the Middle Ages or early modern period
  • Veterinary history or agricultural history writing

If someone uses it in modern writing, they are almost certainly doing so to evoke a sense of the past, or for literary effect. No one says "there's a murrain going around" in a modern news report — they'd say "an outbreak" or "an epidemic."
A quick mental image to anchor it

Picture a medieval English village in winter. One farmer notices his cattle are acting strangely — feverish, refusing to eat. Within days, they're dead. He warns his neighbour. The neighbour's cows start dying too. By the end of the month, three villages have lost most of their livestock. No one knows why. No one can stop it. The animals are dying in their stalls. That unstoppable, mysterious, devastating wave of death sweeping through the animals — that is a murrain.
A murrain is a catastrophic, contagious plague that kills large numbers of farm animals — and, in older English, it was also used as a curse, as in wishing that plague upon someone.
10974:
A muse is a source of creative inspiration — a person, place, or thing that stirs something deep inside an artist, writer, musician, or poet and makes them want to create. When someone has a muse, they don't just feel generally inspired the way you might feel after a good night's sleep. It's stronger than that. A muse lights a specific creative fire that wouldn't exist without it.

Think of it this way: most people can paint a wall. But a muse makes a painter want to paint a masterpiece.
The Two Forms of This Word

"Muse" as a noun has two closely related forms — one with a capital M, and one without.

1. The Muse (capital M) — The Mythological Beings

In ancient Greek and Roman belief, the Muses were nine goddesses who were the divine source of all art, poetry, music, and knowledge. Artists and thinkers believed that creativity didn't come purely from within themselves — it was gifted to them by one of these goddesses. A poet about to write would literally pray to a Muse to "come to" them and fill them with inspiration.

Each Muse governed a specific creative field. For example, one presided over epic poetry, another over music, another over dance, another over comedy, and so on. They were considered sacred, and being touched by a Muse was seen as a divine blessing, not just luck or talent.

This is why, even today, you'll sometimes hear someone say an artist was "touched by the Muse" — it means the work feels almost supernaturally inspired, as if something beyond ordinary human effort produced it.

2. A muse (lowercase m) — The Modern Meaning

Over centuries, this mythological concept came down to earth and became part of everyday language. Today, a muse simply means any real-world person, place, or thing that consistently inspires a creative person to do their best, most passionate work.

It is almost always something personal and specific to the creator — not just any source of inspiration, but their particular source.

This is the most important thing to understand: a muse doesn't just make you feel good or put you in a pleasant mood. A muse unlocks something. It makes an artist access parts of their creativity they couldn't reach otherwise. The work produced under the influence of a muse often feels more alive, more emotionally powerful, and more authentic than work produced without one.

A muse can operate in different ways:

It can be a person. This is the most common usage. A painter might look at someone and feel an overwhelming urge to capture them on canvas — not just once, but again and again, in different lights, moods, and styles. That person is their muse. The muse doesn't necessarily do anything active. They don't teach the artist or tell them what to create. Their mere existence — their face, their energy, their personality, their presence — is enough to fuel the creative act.

It can be a place. A poet might find that a particular city, a landscape, or a childhood home consistently draws poems out of them like water from a well. That place is their muse.

It can be an idea, a memory, or an emotion. Some artists are mused by grief, by longing, by a long-lost relationship, or by a concept they can't stop thinking about.
The Muse as a Person: A Closer Look

Since "a muse" most often refers to a person, it's worth understanding this relationship more deeply, because it has some interesting qualities:

The relationship is often one-sided in a creative sense. The muse may simply be living their life while the artist is obsessively creating work inspired by them. The muse might not even know they are someone's muse.

The muse is not the same as a teacher or a collaborator. A teacher gives you skills. A collaborator works alongside you. A muse simply inspires — their role is passive, even if their effect is enormous.

The muse doesn't have to be a romantic partner, but often is. Many of history's great artistic muses were people the artist deeply loved. The emotional intensity of love is one of the most powerful creative fuels there is. However, a muse can also be a close friend, a family member, a stranger, or even a public figure the artist has never met.

The effect of a muse tends to be ongoing, not a one-time spark. This is what separates a muse from a simple moment of inspiration. You might feel inspired by a sunset once. But a muse keeps inspiring you, repeatedly, across time. They are a well you return to, not a single drink of water.

• The Italian poet Dante wrote some of the greatest literature in history, much of it inspired by a woman named Beatrice, whom he loved deeply. She was his muse — he saw her only a handful of times in his life, but she fueled his creativity for decades.
  • Pablo Picasso, one of the most prolific artists in history, had several muses across his lifetime — different women who inspired distinct periods and styles in his painting. Art historians can actually trace shifts in his style by tracking who his muse was at the time.
  • John Keats, the Romantic poet, was deeply inspired by a woman named Fanny Brawne. She became his muse during some of his most celebrated work.
  • In modern music, artists frequently cite people from their lives as muses — someone who broke their heart, someone they adore, or someone who challenged them, and whose influence is woven through entire albums.
How the Word is Used in Sentences

• "She was his muse — every painting he made during those years had something of her spirit in it."
  • "The city of Paris served as a muse for countless writers and artists throughout the twentieth century."
  • "He had been searching for a new muse since his last great novel — something or someone to reignite his creativity."
  • "She didn't just admire him; she considered him her muse, the reason she wrote at all."
The Subtle Feeling the Word Carries

The word "muse" carries a slightly elevated, almost reverent tone. When someone calls a person their muse, it's a profound compliment — it means you don't just like them or enjoy their company, but that they activate something creative and vital inside you that might otherwise stay dormant. It elevates the subject from "a person I find interesting" to "a person who makes me capable of something greater than myself."

It also carries a hint of mystery and magic — inherited from its mythological roots. Creativity is not fully understood, and the word "muse" honors that mystery. It says: I don't fully know why this person or this place makes me create, but they do, and that power feels almost otherworldly.

A muse (noun) is a source of deep, ongoing creative inspiration — most often a specific person, but sometimes a place or idea — whose existence or presence consistently unlocks and fuels an artist's creativity in a way that feels powerful, personal, and sometimes almost magical. The word descends from nine divine goddesses of the arts in ancient mythology, and even today, it carries that sense of something sacred: the mysterious force that makes great art possible.
10975:
To muse means to think about something in a slow, quiet, and deeply reflective way — without any rush, and often without trying to reach a specific answer or decision.

It is the kind of thinking you do when your mind gently turns something over and over, almost the way you'd turn a smooth stone in your hand — not to break it apart, just to... look at it from every side, slowly.
What Kind of Thinking Is It, Exactly?

This is the most important thing to get right, so let's be precise.

When you muse, your thinking has four key qualities at the same time:

1. It is slow and unhurried.
You are not thinking fast to solve a crisis. There is no pressure. The mind moves gently, at its own pace.

2. It is deep and absorbed.
You are not casually glancing at a thought. You are genuinely lost in it — almost as if the outside world has faded a little.

3. It is reflective.
You are looking inward, or looking back — at a memory, an idea, a feeling, a question about life. It has a thoughtful, meditative quality.

4. It has no urgent goal.
You are not necessarily trying to decide something or solve something. You are simply... dwelling in a thought. Sitting with it.

Think of a person sitting by a window on a rainy afternoon, staring at the drops running down the glass, thinking quietly about whether they made the right choices in life. That person is musing.

"Muse" carries a slightly wistful, dreamy, or wondering quality. It often implies that the person is a little lost in thought — pleasantly or melancholically absorbed. This is why it feels different from simply "thinking" or "considering."

It can be tinged with:

  • nostalgia (thinking about the past)
  • wonder (thinking about something strange or beautiful)
  • gentle uncertainty (thinking about something you don't have an answer to)
How It Is Different from Similar Words

Because English has many "thinking" words, it helps to see exactly where "muse" sits:

  • To think — the most general word. Completely neutral. No texture.
  • To consider — to think about something in order to make a decision. Goal-directed.
  • To ponder — to think carefully and seriously, usually about a problem or a question. More deliberate and effortful than musing.
  • To wonder — to think with curiosity or surprise. More of a spark than a slow simmer.
  • To daydream — to let your mind drift loosely with no real focus. More passive and random than musing.
  • To muse — to think slowly, deeply, and reflectively, with a calm, absorbed, wondering quality. No urgency. No clear goal. Full absorption.

The clearest way to put it: pondering is working hard on a thought; daydreaming is barely holding onto one; musing is somewhere in between — you are genuinely engaged with a thought, but you are not fighting it or forcing it anywhere.
How to Use It in a Sentence (Grammar)

"Muse" is most commonly followed by the prepositions on, upon, over, or about. These prepositions point to what the person is thinking about.

  • She mused on the meaning of friendship.
  • He mused about where his life might have gone differently.
  • They sat quietly, musing over the strange events of the day.
  • She mused upon the vastness of the ocean.

All four prepositions (on / upon / over / about) are correct and carry essentially the same meaning. "Upon" is slightly more formal and literary. "About" is the most casual and everyday.

You can also use it without a preposition, when the object of thought is already clear from context:

  • He stared at the old photograph and mused.
A Special Use: As a Speech Verb

One very common and important use of "muse" is as a speech tag — a word that describes how something was said. When someone says something in a slow, thoughtful, half-to-themselves kind of way, you can write:

  • "I wonder if we ever really know anyone," she mused.
  • "Things might have turned out so differently," he mused.

This signals to the reader that the character is not making a bold statement or asking a direct question — they are speaking softly and reflectively, almost as if thinking aloud. The words are drifting out of their inner world into the air.

Here are several examples that show the full range of how the word is used:

  1. She mused about whether she had been a good mother. (Slow, private, reflective thought — no one to answer her, no urgency)
  2. He sat on the park bench, musing on the nature of time. (Absorbed in a philosophical, wondering kind of thought)
  3. "It's funny how quickly people forget," she mused, staring out the window. (Speaking aloud what she was quietly thinking)
  4. The old professor mused over his student's unusual question for the rest of the evening. (Turning the thought over slowly, not urgently, for a long period)
  5. After the funeral, he walked home slowly, musing on how short a life really is. (A melancholy, inward, reflective kind of thinking)

1. "Muse" is not just "think."
If you say "She mused about what to cook for dinner," it sounds slightly odd — because grocery decisions are too trivial and practical for the slow, absorbed quality that musing implies. Musing suits bigger, deeper, more open-ended subjects: life, time, choices, memory, beauty, loss, meaning.

2. "Muse" is not anxious thinking.
Worrying and musing are opposites in feel. Worrying is tense and circular; musing is calm and open. You muse about the past or the meaning of something — you don't muse about whether you'll miss your flight.

3. "Muse" is slightly literary in tone.
It's a perfectly normal word, but it leans toward the thoughtful and reflective register of language. You'll see it more in writing, literature, and careful speech than in casual everyday conversation.

To muse = to think about something slowly, deeply, calmly, and with full absorption — turning it over in your mind without urgency or a fixed goal, often with a sense of wonder, nostalgia, or quiet uncertainty.
10976: "Mush" has four distinct meanings. Each is explained fully below.
1. A soft, thick, formless mass — food or anything else

This is the most common and central meaning of the word.

As a food term, mush refers to a grain or cereal — most often cornmeal or oats — cooked with water or milk until it becomes a thick, soft, paste-like mass. Think of the texture of oatmeal, grits, or very soft polenta. These are all mush. The defining qualities are: soft enough to hold no firm shape on its own, thick enough that it doesn't flow or pour like a liquid, and often somewhat sticky or gummy.

But mush isn't limited to food. It describes anything — edible or not — that has become soft, wet, pulpy, and shapeless. A very overripe banana that has gone completely soft inside is mush. A piece of bread that has sat in soup long enough to completely absorb it and lose all structure is mush. A cardboard box left out in the rain until it collapses into a wet, formless heap is mush. The essential idea is this: whatever it originally was — firm, structured, solid — it has now been broken down into something soft and undifferentiated, with no clear shape or texture remaining.

The word almost always carries a slightly negative or unappealing tone when used this way. Calling something "mush" implies it has gone past its ideal state — overcooked, oversaturated, or reduced beyond recognition. You rarely describe something as mush and mean it as a compliment.

Examples:

  • "He cooked the oatmeal for too long, and it turned into a grey, tasteless mush."
  • "The vegetables had been boiled into a complete mush — you couldn't tell what they originally were."
  • "After the heavy rain, the paper bag on the doorstep had turned to mush."
  • "The overripe strawberries at the bottom of the punnet were just mush."
2. Excessive sentimentality — in words, writing, or media

In informal usage, "mush" refers to content — usually spoken or written words, a film, a speech, a greeting card, or a gesture — that is excessively sentimental or romantic. Not in a touching way, but in an overdone, cloying, almost embarrassing way. The kind of sweetness that goes so far it stops feeling sincere and starts feeling like a performance.

Think of a romantic film where every line of dialogue is perfectly, artificially tender; or a greeting card that stacks declaration upon declaration of love until it reads more like parody than feeling; or a speech at a wedding that goes on so long about eternal devotion that the audience starts to squirm. That is all "mush."

The word in this sense is almost always used dismissively or teasingly. When someone calls something "mush," they're saying it has crossed the line from genuinely heartfelt into saccharine and excessive — too soft, in a figurative sense, just like overcooked food. It is never a compliment.

Examples:

  • "I can't watch that film — it's pure romantic mush from start to finish."
  • "He meant well, but the anniversary card he wrote came out as complete mush."
  • "She read the letter aloud to her friends, who groaned at all the mush in it."
  • "Cut the mush — just tell me how you actually feel."

Notice how this meaning connects naturally to the first one: just as food becomes mush when it is cooked too far past its ideal point and loses all firm structure, sentiment becomes "mush" when it is pushed too far past genuineness and loses all emotional honesty. Both involve excess leading to a kind of formlessness.

In the specific context of Arctic and subarctic travel — particularly in Alaska, the Yukon Territory, and northern Canada — a "mush" refers to a trip or journey made by dogsled. The person driving the sled is called a musher, and the act of traveling by dogsled is called mushing. When the journey itself is referred to as a noun, it is called a mush.

This meaning is narrow and contextual. You would hear it in discussions of Arctic exploration, wilderness travel, or sled dog racing events such as the Iditarod. Outside of those contexts, it rarely comes up in everyday conversation.

Examples:

  • "The mush from the village to the supply depot covered nearly sixty miles."
  • "She described the three-day mush across the frozen tundra as the most physically demanding thing she had ever done."
  • "The annual mush draws competitors from across North America."

In informal British speech — particularly in certain regional dialects in England — "mush" can mean a person's face. This is purely slang, not used in formal writing or standard speech, but common enough in those dialects to be worth knowing.

Examples:

  • "He got punched right in the mush."
  • "Wipe that look off your mush."

MeaningRegisterHow common

To summarize the four meanings clearly:

Sense 1 — the core, most common meaning — is a soft, thick, formless mass, whether food or any other substance reduced to that state.

Sense 2 — informal — is excessive, overdone sentimentality in words or media.

Sense 3 — specialized — is a dogsled journey in Arctic regions.

Sense 4 — British slang — is a person's face.

Of these, Sense 1 is by far the most frequently used and the one you are most likely to encounter. Sense 2 is common in informal speech and writing. Senses 3 and 4 are narrow and contextual.
10977:
When mushroom is used as a verb, it means to grow, spread, or increase very rapidly — often in a way that feels sudden, large-scale, or hard to control.

Think of how real mushrooms behave in nature: overnight, after rain, they pop up everywhere — quickly, widely, and in large numbers. The verb "mushroom" borrows exactly that image and applies it to anything that grows or spreads in a similarly explosive way.

The verb has two uses that both come from the same core image:

1. To increase or expand very rapidly in number, size, or scope
This is the most common use. When something mushrooms, it goes from small to large very fast — often unexpectedly.

"The small family business mushroomed into a multinational company."
"The problem mushroomed before anyone could address it."
"Online shopping mushroomed during the pandemic."

2. To spread outward and billow into a wide shape (less common but important)
This comes from the visual of a mushroom cloud — something that expands upward and then spreads outward into a wide cap. When smoke, fire, or a cloud mushrooms, it billows and expands into that characteristic shape.

"The smoke mushroomed into the sky after the explosion."
"The flames mushroomed as the fire reached the fuel tanks."

In everyday language, you will encounter the first meaning far more often than the second.

a) The growth is fast, not gradual.
"Mushroom" is not used for slow, steady growth. It implies speed. You wouldn't say a tree mushroomed over 200 years — but you would say a city mushroomed over two decades. Two decades feels fast for a city.

b) The scale is usually large.
There is an element of magnitude. Something goes from relatively small or manageable to large, widespread, or overwhelming.

c) It often carries a sense of surprise or being hard to control.
The growth frequently has an "it happened before anyone fully expected it" quality. Not always alarming, but often surprising.

"What started as a hobby blog mushroomed into a media empire."

d) It can describe both positive and negative growth.
Unlike some words that only carry a negative meaning, "mushroom" is neutral in itself. Whether the mushrooming is good or bad depends on what is mushrooming.

  • Positive: "The movement mushroomed into a global campaign for justice."
  • Negative: "Debt mushroomed after he lost his job."
  • Neutral: "The city's population has mushroomed over the last decade."

e) It is intransitive — things mushroom on their own.
You do not "mushroom something." You cannot say "The company mushroomed its profits." Instead, the subject itself does the mushrooming: "Their profits mushroomed." The action happens to the subject, not to an object.

FormExample
BaseProblems mushroom quickly in poorly managed systems.
-ing (present participle)The crowd was mushrooming by the minute.
-ed (past tense)The costs mushroomed beyond the original budget.
Third person singularEvery time it rains, the list of complaints mushrooms.
Common Contexts Where You'll See It

"Mushroom" as a verb appears very frequently in:

  • News and journalism: "The conflict mushroomed into a full-scale war."
  • Business and economics: "The startup mushroomed from 10 to 10,000 users in a month."
  • Social and political writing: "Opposition mushroomed across the country."
  • Everyday speech: "My to-do list just keeps mushrooming!"
How to Know You're Using It Correctly

Ask yourself: Is there something that started small (or manageable) and then rapidly grew large, widespread, or out of control? If yes, "mushroom" fits perfectly.

If the growth is slow and steady (like a plant growing across seasons), "mushroom" would feel out of place. Use it only when you want to convey speed, scale, and that sense of sudden expansion.
One Final Sentence That Captures Everything

"A single spark mushroomed into a wildfire that swept across three states."

Read that sentence and you can feel the word working — one small thing, then sudden, uncontrollable, large-scale growth. That is the verb "mushroom" in its fullest sense.
10978: Mushy means soft and without firm shape — either physically or emotionally.

When something is mushy, it is soft, wet, and squishable. It gives way easily under pressure. It is not solid, not liquid — it is that unpleasant in-between state where something has lost the firmness it should have.

Think of:

  • Overcooked vegetables that have turned limp and soggy
  • A banana left too long — it goes brown and squishes between your fingers
  • Wet mud under your boots
  • Porridge or mashed potatoes
  • A fruit that has started to rot and feels soft when you press it

The physical sense almost always carries a slightly negative or undesirable feeling. Things become mushy when they should not be — vegetables that were supposed to be crisp, fruit that was supposed to be firm. The mushiness is usually caused by too much moisture, too much heat, or decay over time.

Example sentences:

  • "Don't overcook the broccoli — it goes mushy."
  • "The ground was mushy after the rain."
  • "These strawberries have gone mushy; throw them away."

This is the figurative use, and it is very common in everyday English.

When a person, a movie, a song, or a moment is described as mushy, it means it is overly soft with emotion — excessively sentimental, tender, romantic, or lovey-dovey. It is when feelings are expressed in a sweet, heartfelt way that feels a bit over the top or uncomfortably intense for the observer.

Think of:

  • A couple who keep saying "I love you so much, you're my whole world" in front of others
  • A film that makes you cry with extremely emotional scenes and soft music
  • A birthday card filled with sweet, gushing poetry about how wonderful you are
  • A friend who hugs you for too long and gets teary while telling you how much your friendship means

The emotional sense, like the physical one, carries a gentle sense of excess. A little sentiment is touching; too much becomes mushy. There is often a slight eye-roll implied — "oh, stop being so mushy" — though it is not a harsh criticism. It is more affectionate teasing than genuine disapproval.

Example sentences:

  • "He gets so mushy at weddings — he was crying the whole time."
  • "I can't watch this film with you; it's too mushy for me."
  • "She wrote him a very mushy love letter."
  • "Stop being mushy and just tell me what time you'll arrive."
The Key Feeling Behind Both Meanings

Notice how both meanings share the same core idea: something that has lost its shape and gone soft in an excessive way.

Physically — a firm vegetable collapses into a soft, formless blob.
Emotionally — a composed person collapses into tears and sentimentality.

In both cases, there is a sense that boundaries have melted away. This is why the same word works for both.

Mushy is not a strongly negative word. It is gentle in its criticism.

When used for physical things, it simply describes an undesirable texture — no strong judgment, just a description of something that has gone softer than it should.

When used for emotional things, it is usually said with a smile or a light tease. Calling someone mushy does not mean they are ridiculous; it means they are being openly and perhaps excessively soft-hearted. Many people find mushy moments sweet, even if they feel a little awkward watching them.

Occasionally, you may see "mushy" applied to ideas or reasoning — meaning unclear, imprecise, or lacking sharpness. "Mushy thinking" means fuzzy logic that has no firm structure. This use is less common in everyday conversation but appears in writing and criticism.

Example: "The policy paper was full of mushy generalities and no real plan."

SituationWhat "mushy" means

If something physical is mushy → it is soft, wet, and lost its firm shape.
If a person or moment is mushy → it is overly sentimental, tender, and emotionally soft.
If an idea is mushy → it is vague and lacking clarity.

The common thread in all uses: softness that has crossed into excess.
10979:
When something is "music to one's ears," it means that what you heard (or read, or were told) was extremely pleasing, welcome, or exactly what you were hoping to hear.

It describes that feeling of relief, happiness, or satisfaction you get when you receive good news, a compliment, a positive answer, or any information that makes you feel instantly better.
Breaking It Down Simply

Think about how you feel when you hear your favourite song after a long, tiring day. It just feels right. It soothes you. It makes you happy instantly.

Now imagine that same feeling — but caused by words instead of actual music.

Maybe your boss says, "You're getting a promotion." Or a doctor says, "Everything looks perfectly fine." Or a friend says, "Yes, I'll help you."

That feeling of joy, relief, and delight at hearing those words — that is what this idiom captures. The words feel as beautiful and satisfying as music does to a music lover.

So the idiom takes the joy of music and uses it as a comparison for the joy of hearing something wonderful.
The Structure of the Idiom

The full form is:

"That is music to my/one's/his/her ears."

The word "one's" simply changes depending on who is feeling the pleasure:

  • Music to my ears — you are the one who is pleased.
  • Music to his/her ears — someone else is pleased.
  • Music to their ears — a group of people are pleased.

You will almost always see it used with the verb "to be" (is, was, were):

  • "That news was music to my ears."
  • "Your words are music to my ears."
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The idiom has been in use in the English language for centuries. The idea behind it is ancient and universal: music has always been considered one of the most beautiful and pleasing things a human being can experience. Across all cultures and throughout history, music has represented joy, celebration, and emotional comfort.

So when people started using it as an idiom, they were essentially saying: "What I just heard felt as beautiful and satisfying as music."

William Shakespeare, writing in the late 1500s and early 1600s, used similar imagery — comparing the pleasure of hearing something wonderful to the pleasure of hearing beautiful music. This shows the idea has been deeply embedded in the English-speaking mind for a very long time.

Over time, this comparison became a fixed idiom, a set phrase that people use without necessarily thinking about music at all.
Real-Life Examples

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally it fits:

At work:

After months of hard work, hearing the manager say "You did an outstanding job" was music to my ears.

At school:

When the teacher announced the exam was postponed, it was music to every student's ears.

At the doctor's:

"Your test results are completely normal" — those six words were pure music to his ears.

In everyday life:

She had been waiting all week for her best friend to say "I forgive you." When she finally heard it, it was music to her ears.

With money:

"Your loan has been approved." I can't tell you how much music that was to my ears.

In a family setting:

When my son called to say he had landed safely, it was music to my ears.

Notice in all these examples, the person desperately wanted to hear that thing — and when they finally did, the relief and happiness felt as beautiful as music.
The Emotion Behind the Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a sense of relief mixed with joy. It is not just about hearing something pleasant casually — it tends to be used when:

  • You were anxious or worried and the good news put your mind at rest.
  • You were hoping for a specific answer and you finally got it.
  • You received praise or validation that you really needed.
  • Something turned out better than you feared.

This emotional weight — the relief, the gratitude, the happiness — is what makes this idiom so expressive. Plain words like "I was happy to hear that" do not quite capture the depth of the feeling the way this idiom does.
Tone and Register

This is a neutral-to-warm idiom. It is:

  • Perfectly fine in everyday casual conversation.
  • Acceptable in semi-formal writing and speech.
  • Genuine and heartfelt, not sarcastic (in standard usage).

It is not rude, not overly formal, and not slang. You can use it when speaking to a friend, a colleague, a teacher, or even in a written message.
Can It Be Used Sarcastically?

Yes, occasionally. In spoken English, tone of voice can flip its meaning:

"Oh, so you're saying I have to work on the weekend? Music to my ears, truly."

Said with a flat or bitter tone, this means the opposite — the news is awful and very unwelcome. But this sarcastic use is secondary. The primary and most common use is sincere and positive.

As a learner, stick to using it sincerely until you are very comfortable with English sarcasm.
Common Variations

You may encounter slightly different phrasings that mean the same thing:

  • "That's music to my ears!" — the most common, everyday version.
  • "Pure music to my ears" — with "pure" added for extra emphasis.
  • "Sweet music to my ears" — "sweet" reinforces the pleasantness.
  • "Like music to my ears" — some people add "like" to make the comparison explicit.

All of these carry the same meaning. The core phrase is always "music to (someone's) ears."
Similar Idioms (for Context)

Knowing related idioms helps you understand the family this one belongs to:

  • "A breath of fresh air" — something refreshing and welcome (but more about a person or situation, not specifically about news you hear).
  • "A feast for the eyes" — something visually beautiful (the same pattern: a sensory pleasure used as a comparison for delight).
  • "Sweet nothings" — kind, affectionate words whispered to someone (related to the pleasure of hearing loving words).
  • "Fall on deaf ears" — when something said is ignored or not listened to (an opposite idea: words that bring no pleasure or response).
How to Use It Yourself

When you want to use this idiom, ask yourself:

  1. Did someone just tell me (or someone else) something really good?
  2. Was there a sense of waiting, hoping, or worrying before that news?
  3. Does the news bring genuine relief, happiness, or satisfaction?

If yes to these, you can naturally say:

"That was music to my ears."

or

"I'm sure that'll be music to her ears."
Quick Summary

MeaningSomething you hear that is extremely pleasing, welcome, or exactly what you hoped to hear
Feeling it describesJoy, relief, and deep satisfaction upon hearing good news
OriginThe universal human pleasure of music used as a metaphor for the pleasure of hearing wonderful words
ToneSincere, warm, positive (can be sarcastic with the right tone)
Most common form"That is/was music to my ears."

In short: whenever words or news make your heart lift the way a beautiful song does, that moment is perfectly described as music to your ears.
